items.title: From nonmagnetic to magnetic: A 2D semiconductor with electrically tunable magnetism
items.summary: Researchers from the National University of Singapore (NUS), in collaboration with scientists from institutions in Switzerland, the Czech Republic and Germany, have demonstrated a way to introduce magnetism into an otherwise nonmagnetic two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor and subsequently control its magnetic properties using an electrical voltage. The findings, published in Science Advances, establish a new platform for investigating electrically controllable magnetism in atomically thin materials, with potential implications for future spintronic technologies.

items.title: Data-driven cricket ratings could reveal undervalued batters and bowlers through peer comparisons
items.summary: An analytical method could help high-level cricket franchises make more informed decisions about player recruitment, retention and team selection, according to research published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management. The approach uses data envelopment analysis (DEA) to compare efficiency using multiple inputs and outputs. In the world of cricket, this means assessing players against their peers rather than relying on individual statistics.

Alton Military Prison Site in Alton, Illinois
items.summary: Alton, Illinois's State Penitentiary officially opened in 1833, making it the first state prison in Illinois. It was used to incarcerate convicted criminals from across the state and later served as a military prison. During the Civil War, the facility became the Alton Military Prison and was used to hold Confederate prisoners of war. More than 11,000 Confederate soldiers were held there before the prison closed. Les Houthis ont affirmé avoir visé l’aéroport King Khalid ainsi que la ville de Khamis Mushait. La série d’attaques menée ces derniers jours contre le royaume a fait 18 morts. Le mouvement yéménite avait également revendiqué des frappes contre l’aéroport de Dammam et des installations énergétiques du géant Aramco.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.12599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse computation can scale the parametric capacity of LLMs without proportionally increasing active computation, but pretraining sparse architectures remains expensive and data-hungry. items.title: [Comment] Offline: Medicine for peace
items.summary: Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) is most famous for his line in Leviathan (1651) that, “the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”. That proposition may have been true in 17th-century England, but, thanks to the evolution and expansion of health systems, it is not so today for many, although obviously not all. But abstracting that line alone is to miss Hobbes’ wider views about the nature of human being. He believed that without a “common power” ruling over society, our natural tendency is “that condition which is called war…of every man against every man”.

items.title: [Correspondence] Personalising maintenance after tirzepatide weight loss

However, the trial's mean effects might not fully convey an important clinical message: response to lower-dose maintenance was heterogeneous.

items.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial

Estimated reductions in the incidence and mortality of colorectal cancer were much lower than anticipated at trial design.

items.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial
items.summary: The NordICC trial1 should be considered in context with previous colorectal cancer screening studies.2,3 Four randomised controlled trials with more than 458 000 participants show consistent colorectal cancer incidence reductions of 18–23% and larger colorectal cancer mortality reductions of 22–31% with sigmoidoscopy (appendix).3 In the NordICC trial, screening reduced colorectal cancer incidence but not mortality.1

items.title: Fort Breendonk in Willebroek, Belgium
items.summary: Fort van Breendonk is a transit camp and WWII Nazi Prison in Willebroek, Belgium. It was originally built between 1906 and 1913 and has been used in both World War I and World War II. It was used as a prison camp for the detention of political prisoners, resistance members, and Jews. It became known for the poor living conditions rather than the many deaths. The camp had more SS guards than prisoners, which meant they were constantly watched. Many prisoners were transported to larger concentration camps in Europe. The fort has held 3,590 prisoners, 303 of whom died in the camp, 1,741 passed away in other camps before the end of the war. The camp was eventually evacuated by September 1944, by the Allies of World War II.
